posts.title: Agent reliability is a data problem
posts.hook: Most agent failures aren't model failures. They're context failures.
posts.body:
Most agent failures aren't model failures. They're context failures.

I've been running Claude Code agents across my entire GTM stack for months now. Enrichment, email infrastructure, CRM writes, content ops. The pattern is clear.

When an agent breaks, 9 times out of 10 it's one of three things:

1. The context window got polluted with irrelevant state
2. The instructions were ambiguous about which account/credential to use
3. There was no verification step before the agent declared "done"

None of those are model intelligence problems. They're engineering problems.

I keep a lessons.md file that every agent session reads on startup. Every time an agent makes a mistake, the rule goes in the file. Wrong Vercel project? Rule. Wrong Gmail account? Rule. Deployed without building first? Rule.

My agent failure rate dropped by maybe 70% just from that file getting longer.

The teams building "agent reliability platforms" are solving a real problem. But the unsexy version is... a markdown file, a preflight checklist, and forcing your agent to prove its work before marking done.

Reliability isn't a model parameter. It's an ops discipline.
posts.cta: What's your most common agent failure mode? Genuinely curious if others see the same context pollution pattern.

remixes.label: garbage-in-garbage-out
remixes.hook: Your agent isn't stupid. You're feeding it noise.
remixes.body:
Your agent isn't stupid. You're feeding it noise.

I spent three months debugging agent failures across enrichment pipelines, CRM automations, and content workflows. I kept blaming the model. Tried different prompts. Tried different temperatures. Tried chain-of-thought tricks.

The actual fix every single time? Better input data.

One pipeline was failing because it ingested a 4,000-token CRM record when the agent only needed three fields. Another broke because two conflicting instructions lived in different config files. A third hallucinated because the retrieval step returned semantically similar but factually wrong context.

The model was fine. The plumbing around it was leaking.

Here's what I do now before blaming the model:

1. Log the exact context window contents at failure time. Not what I think went in. What actually went in.
2. Measure signal-to-noise ratio. If less than 30% of the context is relevant to the task, trim first.
3. Treat instructions like code. Version them. Test them. Don't let ambiguity ship.

Agent reliability is an information architecture problem. The sooner you treat it that way, the sooner your agents stop surprising you.

remixes.label: ops-not-prompts
remixes.hook: The best prompt engineer I know doesn't write prompts. She writes data contracts.
remixes.body:
The best prompt engineer I know doesn't write prompts. She writes data contracts.

She runs a 12-agent system for a Series B company's entire post-sale workflow. Onboarding, usage tracking, renewal signals, churn prediction. When I asked how she keeps it reliable, she pulled up a spreadsheet.

Not a prompt library. A schema registry.

Every agent has a defined input contract: exactly which fields it receives, their types, and their freshness requirements. Every agent has an output contract: what it returns, what downstream agents expect, and what happens when a field is null.

When something breaks, she doesn't tweak the prompt. She checks which contract was violated. Nine out of ten times, an upstream agent changed its output shape or a data source went stale.

This is the part most teams skip. They obsess over the reasoning step and ignore the data step. But agents don't fail because they can't reason. They fail because they're reasoning over the wrong inputs.

Treat your agent context like an API contract and reliability becomes a solved problem.

posts.title: 3 engineers and Claude Code to $1M ARR
posts.hook: 3 engineers hitting $1M ARR in 11 months isn't a flex. It's the new baseline.
posts.body:
3 engineers hitting $1M ARR in 11 months isn't a flex. It's the new baseline.

I'm watching this pattern repeat across every founder I talk to. Small teams with coding agents are outshipping teams 5x their size. Not because they're smarter. Because the bottleneck moved.

It used to be: idea --> hire engineers --> build for months --> ship --> iterate.

Now it's: idea --> Claude Code session --> working prototype same day --> ship --> iterate with agents.

The constraint isn't engineering capacity anymore. It's taste. Knowing what to build. Knowing when to stop adding features. Knowing which problem actually matters.

I build my entire GTM engine this way. Enrichment pipelines, email warmup infrastructure, CRM automation, content distribution. One person. Coding agents. SQLite. APIs.

remixes.hook: The bottleneck in startups used to be engineering capacity. Now it's decision speed.
remixes.body:
The bottleneck in startups used to be engineering capacity. Now it's decision speed.

I keep meeting 2-4 person teams shipping faster than the 20-person companies I worked with five years ago. Same complexity. Same markets. Wildly different velocity.

The obvious explanation is coding agents. Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot. And yes, those matter. But that's not the real unlock.

The real unlock is that small teams make decisions in minutes instead of weeks. There's no sprint planning meeting to schedule the feature. No architecture review board. No PM writing a spec that an engineer rewrites anyway.

The founder says "we need this." They open a Claude Code session. It ships that afternoon.

Coding agents didn't just compress the build phase. They eliminated the organizational overhead that made building slow in the first place. Every meeting about what to build, how to build it, and when to ship it. Gone.

This is why headcount is becoming a liability, not an asset, for early-stage teams. Every person you add re-introduces coordination cost. And coordination cost is now the dominant bottleneck.

Three engineers with agents aren't just coding faster. They're deciding faster. And in startups, decision speed is everything.

Compare that to the 2021 playbook: raise a seed round, hire 8 engineers, spend 6 months building v1, launch to crickets, run out of runway.

This isn't about AI replacing engineers. It's about the minimum viable team getting dramatically smaller. The founders who internalize this will build faster, stay leaner, and keep more equity.

posts.title: MCP is plumbing not magic
posts.hook: MCP is just plumbing. That's exactly why it works.
posts.body:
MCP is just plumbing. That's exactly why it works.

I was a plumber for ten years before tech. The thing about plumbing is nobody cares about it until it breaks. And the best plumbing is the kind you never think about.

MCP is the same. It's a standard way for agents to talk to tools. Not glamorous. Not a breakthrough in reasoning. Just a clean interface contract.

I have MCP servers connected to my CRM, email platform, browser automation, design tools. My agent doesn't need custom integration code for each one. It discovers what's available and calls it.

The 90% that get it wrong? They're treating MCP like a feature instead of infrastructure. Exposing too many tools without scoping permissions. Letting agents write to production without guardrails. No credential routing.

My setup forces a preflight check before any write operation. Which workspace. Which identity. Which credential store. The agent has to echo it back before proceeding.

Boring? Yes. But I haven't accidentally sent an email from the wrong account in months.

The best tool integrations are the ones your agent uses without you noticing. That's the whole point.

remixes.label: plumber-to-protocol
remixes.hook: I laid pipe for a decade. Now I build protocols that let AI agents talk to databases. The job is the same.
remixes.body:
I laid pipe for a decade. Now I build protocols that let AI agents talk to databases. The job is the same.

In plumbing, the work that matters is invisible. Nobody tours their house pointing at copper joints. But the moment a joint leaks, everything downstream breaks.

MCP is the same kind of work. It's a protocol. A standard way to connect an AI agent to a tool. It defines what the tool can do, what inputs it expects, and what it returns. Clean interface. No ambiguity.

Before MCP, every agent-to-tool connection was custom. You'd write bespoke API wrappers, handle auth differently for each service, and pray the output format didn't change. It was like running a different pipe fitting for every fixture in the house.

Now I have one protocol for Attio, Gmail, Customer.io, Typefully, and a dozen other tools. Same connection pattern. Same error handling. Same way to discover what's available.

The people chasing "AGI breakthroughs" don't understand this. Infrastructure wins are boring. But boring infrastructure is what turns a demo into a production system.

I've watched too many smart people skip the plumbing and wonder why their agent works in a notebook but breaks in production. The answer is always the same: you built the faucet but forgot the pipes.
remixes.cta: What's the most boring piece of infrastructure that made your agent system actually work?

remixes.label: standards-win
remixes.hook: USB won. Bluetooth won. HTTP won. MCP is next. Standards always beat clever hacks.
remixes.body:
USB won. Bluetooth won. HTTP won. MCP is next. Standards always beat clever hacks.

Every decade, some new technology emerges and everyone builds their own proprietary way to use it. Then a standard shows up, looks boring, and slowly wins because it reduces the integration cost to near zero.

That's MCP for AI agents.

Six months ago, connecting Claude to my CRM required a custom tool definition, hand-rolled auth, and a prayer that the API wouldn't change. Connecting it to Gmail was a different integration. Customer.io, another one. Each tool was its own snowflake.

Now they're all MCP servers. Same discovery protocol. Same tool schema. Same way to handle permissions. When I add a new tool, I don't write integration code. I point the agent at an MCP endpoint and it figures out what's available.

The people dismissing MCP as "just JSON-RPC" are technically correct and strategically wrong. HTTP was "just a text protocol." USB was "just a connector standard." The value isn't in the specification. It's in the ecosystem that forms around it.

I'm running MCP servers with actual write access to production systems. CRM updates, email sends, content publishing. The protocol is simple enough that I trust it with real operations. That's the bar for infrastructure. Not impressive. Trustworthy.

posts.title: After the AI SDR books the meeting
posts.hook: AI SDRs can book meetings. Nobody talks about what happens in the 48 hours after.
posts.body:
AI SDRs can book meetings. Nobody talks about what happens in the 48 hours after.

The meeting books. The AE gets a calendar invite with a company name and a title. Maybe a one-line summary. Then they spend 20 minutes scrambling through LinkedIn, the CRM, and Google trying to figure out who this person is and why they took the meeting.

That gap between "meeting booked" and "AE is actually prepared" is where deals die quietly.

What I'm building instead: the moment a meeting books, an enrichment pipeline fires. Company data, tech stack signals, recent funding, org chart, any existing touchpoints in the CRM, intent signals from the last 30 days. All of it lands in a structured brief the AE reads in 90 seconds.

The pipeline is Claude Code + a few API calls + SQLite. No enterprise platform. No $40k/year "sales intelligence" contract.

The AI SDR conversation is focused on the wrong end of the funnel. Booking meetings was never the hard part. Converting them was.

If your AI SDR books 3x more meetings but your close rate drops by half, you just built an expensive calendar filler.

Your AI SDR just booked a meeting. Your AE is about to waste the first 5 minutes apologizing for not knowing anything about the prospect.

This is the dirty secret of the AI SDR boom. The booking rate goes up. The conversion rate stays flat. And nobody connects the dots.

Here's what's happening in the 48 hours between booking and meeting at most companies: the AE gets a calendar invite with a name and a company. Maybe a one-liner from the AI about why they responded. The AE then spends 15-20 minutes on LinkedIn, the CRM, and Google trying to build context.

Except they're also prepping for three other meetings. So they skim. They miss that the prospect mentioned a specific pain point in the email thread. They don't notice the prospect's company just raised a round. They walk in cold and generic.

The prospect notices. First impressions are permanent.

The irony is painful. We automated the hardest part of sales development (getting someone to say yes to a meeting) and then we fumble the handoff with manual research and scrambled prep.

The fix isn't complicated. When the meeting books, trigger an enrichment pipeline. Pull firmographics, recent news, tech stack, the actual email thread that led to the booking, any CRM history. Package it into a one-page brief that lands in the AE's inbox immediately.

Automate the setup, not just the ask.

The AI SDR space exploded this year. Booking rates are up. Response rates are improving. The top of funnel is wider than ever.

But conversion rates from meeting to opportunity? Flat. Sometimes down.

I see this with every team I work with. They invested in automated outbound and forgot that the meeting itself is where revenue happens. The AE walks in underprepped because nobody built the bridge between "meeting booked" and "AE has full context."

What that bridge looks like in practice:

At booking time, a pipeline fires. It pulls the prospect's LinkedIn activity, company news from the last 90 days, tech stack from BuiltWith, any existing CRM touchpoints, and the full email thread that generated the meeting. It scores the account against your ICP. It generates a one-page brief with the top three talking points based on what the prospect actually cares about.

That brief hits the AE's inbox and Slack within minutes of the booking.

The AE walks in knowing the prospect's world. The first five minutes feel like a warm conversation, not a cold discovery call.

This is a two-day build with the right enrichment stack. It's not hard. It's just not where people are looking.

posts.title: GTM engineering isn't Clay power usage
posts.hook: If your entire GTM engineering stack is Clay tables, you're a power user, not an engineer.
posts.body:
If your entire GTM engineering stack is Clay tables, you're a power user, not an engineer.

I like Clay. I've used Clay. But there's a ceiling.

When your enrichment provider returns garbage data, can you swap it out in 10 minutes? When you need to cross-reference three data sources and score based on custom logic, are you fighting a no-code UI to do it? When your outbound volume needs to scale 10x, does your per-record pricing scale with you?

GTM engineering means owning the pipeline. Enrichment sources you can swap. Scoring logic in code you can version control. A database you query directly instead of exporting CSVs.

My stack: Python scripts calling enrichment APIs directly. SQLite as the warehouse. Claude Code for the orchestration layer. Total cost is API usage. No per-seat, no per-record, no platform fee.

When Clearbit's data quality dropped, I swapped to a different provider in one afternoon. Changed the API call, mapped the fields, reran the pipeline. In Clay that's rebuilding half your tables.

The point isn't anti-Clay. It's that the GTM engineer title should mean you can build the thing from scratch if you had to. The tool is a choice, not a dependency.

remixes.hook: There's a spectrum between no-code power user and GTM engineer. Most people don't know where they sit on it.
remixes.body:
There's a spectrum between no-code power user and GTM engineer. Most people don't know where they sit on it.

I'm not here to trash Clay or any no-code tool. They solve real problems and they solve them fast. The question is what happens when the problem outgrows the tool.

Power user: you can build complex workflows inside a platform. You know the shortcuts, the hidden features, the workarounds. But you're renting capability. The platform decides what's possible.

GTM engineer: you can build the workflow from primitives. When an enrichment provider returns bad data, you swap it in an hour. When you need custom scoring logic that doesn't fit a dropdown, you write it. When volume scales 10x, you don't hit a pricing wall.

Neither is wrong. But they're different jobs with different ceilings.

The problem I see is people calling themselves GTM engineers who've never written a script, never touched an API directly, never debugged a data pipeline. They're power users with an inflated title.

And power users hit walls. The enrichment provider changes their API. The no-code platform removes a feature. The volume gets expensive. Every time, they're stuck waiting for the platform to fix it.

GTM engineering means owning your stack deeply enough to fix it yourself. That requires code. Not a lot of code. But some. And the willingness to learn.
remixes.cta: Where do you sit on the spectrum? Power user, engineer, or somewhere in between?

remixes.label: clay-ceiling-story
remixes.hook: I hit the Clay ceiling at 2 AM during a campaign launch. That's when I stopped being a power user.
remixes.body:
I hit the Clay ceiling at 2 AM during a campaign launch. That's when I stopped being a power user.

The enrichment step was returning 40% garbage. Names matched to wrong companies. Titles from two jobs ago. Emails that bounced on send. I needed to cross-reference against a second provider, filter by a custom ICP score, and deduplicate across three lists.

In Clay, that's a nightmare of nested formulas, manual column checks, and hoping the waterfall enrichment doesn't timeout. At 2 AM with a campaign going live at 6 AM, I wasn't going to make it.

So I wrote a Python script. Pulled the same data from the API directly. Added a second enrichment source. Wrote the scoring logic I actually needed. Deduped in pandas. Had clean data by 3:30 AM.

That script still runs. I've modified it a dozen times since. Added new data sources, changed scoring weights, plugged in different providers when one went down. Each change took minutes because I own the code.

The Clay table? I would have rebuilt it from scratch every time.

This isn't anti-Clay. Clay is great for prototyping and simple workflows. But there's a ceiling. And if you're doing GTM engineering at any real scale, you're going to hit it.

The question is whether you can build your way past it or whether you're stuck waiting for the platform to raise the ceiling for you.

posts.title: LinkedIn organic compounding is real
posts.hook: I can trace actual pipeline back to LinkedIn posts from 4 months ago. Not impressions. Pipeline.
posts.body:
I can trace actual pipeline back to LinkedIn posts from 4 months ago. Not impressions. Pipeline.

Someone reads a post in March. They don't engage. They bookmark it or just remember the name. In July they have the exact problem I described. They come inbound.

You can't attribute this in a dashboard. There's no UTM. There's no click trail. They just show up and say "I've been following your posts."

This is the part of content strategy that doesn't fit in a spreadsheet but absolutely shows up in revenue.

What makes it work isn't posting frequency. It's posting substance. Every post needs to teach something specific enough that someone could go implement it. Not "AI is changing sales." More like "here's the exact enrichment pipeline I built, here's what it costs, here's the SQLite schema."

The compound effect comes from being the person who actually shows how things work instead of just commenting that things are changing.

I post almost daily. Some posts get 200 views. Some get 5,000. Doesn't matter. The ones that convert to pipeline are almost never the ones with the most impressions. They're the ones where the right person saw them at the right time.

Consistency plus substance. That's the whole strategy.

I closed a deal last month. Discovery call felt like a formality. They already knew my process, my pricing philosophy, even a specific project I'd written about. When I asked how they found me, the answer was "I've been reading your stuff for a while."

No form fill. No webinar registration. No content download. Just months of posts building a mental model of what I do and why I do it that way.

This is the dark funnel. It's not mysterious. It's just untrackable by conventional tools. Someone reads 15 of your posts over 4 months. They tell a colleague. That colleague has a budget. They Google your name directly.

The attribution model says it was "direct traffic." The reality is it was 4 months of consistent, specific content that built enough trust to skip the typical evaluation process.

I stopped trying to measure this and started trusting the pattern. Post consistently about real problems you solve. Be specific enough that people remember your name when the problem hits. The pipeline shows up on its own timeline.

A LinkedIn post has a 48-hour shelf life. Unless it doesn't.

Most content dies after the algorithm stops pushing it. But some posts keep working for months because they describe a specific problem so precisely that when someone finally encounters that problem, they remember who wrote about it.

I wrote a post about a niche outbound problem back in March. Engagement was fine, nothing viral. Four months later someone booked a call and opened with "you wrote that thing about sequences that actually matched what we're dealing with."

This is the compounding effect nobody talks about. Each post you write that's specific enough to be memorable becomes a node in someone's mental map. Over time, you're not competing for attention. You're the name that surfaces when the timing is right.

The catch: generic posts don't compound. "5 tips for better marketing" evaporates in 24 hours. "Here's exactly how I fixed a broken email deliverability setup for a 200-person sales team" lives in someone's memory until they have the same problem.

Specificity is the interest rate on content. The more specific, the longer it compounds.

posts.title: Build the boring thing first
posts.hook: Spent a week building an AI-powered lead scoring model. The feature that actually moved the needle? A CSV export button.
posts.body:
Spent a week building an AI-powered lead scoring model. The feature that actually moved the needle? A CSV export button.

This keeps happening. The sophisticated thing you think will impress people sits unused. The dead-simple thing that saves them 10 minutes a day gets used every morning.

I built an entire content distribution system with Discord webhooks, automated dispatching, multi-platform formatting. The feature my workflow actually depends on most? A plain text clipboard copy.

The pattern is always the same. You build the impressive thing because it's interesting to build. Then you watch people ignore it and ask for the thing you could've shipped in an hour.

Now I have a rule: before building anything clever, ship the boring version first. Does it work as a script someone runs manually? Does it work as a spreadsheet? Does it work as a markdown file?

If the boring version solves the problem, you're done. Move on. Build the next boring thing.

The AI feature can come later, after you know people actually use the workflow. Most of the time they won't need it. The CSV export was enough.

remixes.hook: The more complex my solution, the less my users care. This pattern has repeated five times now.
remixes.body:
The more complex my solution, the less my users care. This pattern has repeated five times now.

I built a multi-platform content distribution system. Automated dispatching, Discord webhooks, format conversion across 6 channels. Took weeks. The thing people actually love? A button that copies clean text to their clipboard.

I built an enrichment pipeline with 4 data providers, scoring algorithms, deduplication logic. The thing that gets used daily? A filtered CSV download.

I built an AI-powered analytics dashboard with trend detection. The thing people screenshot and share? A single number on the homepage.

There's a pattern here and it's humbling. Users don't want sophisticated. They want solved. And "solved" almost always looks embarrassingly simple from the builder's perspective.

The gap is that builders optimize for technical impressiveness because that's what earns peer respect. Users optimize for "does this save me time right now." Those two things almost never overlap.

Now I start every feature by asking: what's the dumbest version of this that would still be useful? Build that first. If nobody uses it, the smart version wouldn't have helped either. If everyone uses it, maybe the smart version is unnecessary.

remixes.label: minimum-viable-magic
remixes.hook: Your users don't want AI. They want to go home 30 minutes earlier.
remixes.body:
Your users don't want AI. They want to go home 30 minutes earlier.

I learned this after building an AI-powered lead scoring model that sat unused while a CSV export button I added as an afterthought became the most-used feature in the product.

The scoring model was technically impressive. It analyzed 12 signals, weighted them dynamically, produced a score with confidence intervals. Beautiful engineering. Nobody opened that tab.

The CSV button let someone download their list, paste it into a spreadsheet they already trusted, and move on with their day. Ten seconds saved, repeated every morning.

This is the gap between what builders find interesting and what users find valuable. We chase complexity because it feels like progress. Users chase simplicity because they have 47 other things to do today.

The best product instinct I've developed: watch what people do with your output. If they're exporting it, screenshotting it, or copy-pasting it somewhere else, that "somewhere else" is where the real workflow lives. Build for that destination, not for keeping them in your app.

Boring features that save 10 minutes a day beat impressive features that require 10 minutes to learn.

posts.title: Kill the 14-step sequence
posts.hook: 14-step outbound sequences are a relic of the "more touches = more pipeline" era. That era is over.
posts.body:
14-step outbound sequences are a relic of the "more touches = more pipeline" era. That era is over.

Every inbox is drowning. Your prospect gets 30 cold emails a day. Touch 9 of 14 isn't persistence. It's noise.

I run 3-touch sequences now. Sometimes 2. The entire bet is on the first email being relevant enough that a follow-up is welcome, not annoying.

How do you make the first email that good? You do the work upfront.

Enrichment that actually tells you something useful. Not just company size and industry. What tech they run. What they posted about last week. What job they just opened. What their competitor just launched.

Then you write one email that connects your thing to their actual situation. Not a template with {firstName} and {companyName} swapped in. An email that couldn't have been sent to anyone else.

The infrastructure to do this at scale is the hard part. Enrichment APIs, scoring logic, dynamic personalization blocks, deliverability monitoring. That's where the engineering goes.

Not into writing email 11 of 14 that says "just bumping this to the top of your inbox."

Fewer touches, better research, higher conversion. The math works every time.

remixes.label: first-email-or-nothing
remixes.hook: If your first cold email isn't good enough to get a reply, sending 13 more won't fix it.
remixes.body:
If your first cold email isn't good enough to get a reply, sending 13 more won't fix it.

The entire outbound industry built itself on a volume assumption: more touches equals more pipeline. So we got 14-step sequences, 21-day cadences, and "just checking in" follow-ups that train your prospects to ignore you.

Here's what actually changed my reply rates. I stopped writing sequences and started writing first emails.

All the effort goes into email one. Research the company. Find a specific, timely reason to reach out. Write something that proves you understand their situation. Make the ask small and clear.

If that email doesn't land, a follow-up saying "bumping this to the top of your inbox" isn't going to change their mind. They saw it. They decided it wasn't relevant. More volume doesn't fix a relevance problem.

I run 2 to 3 touch sequences now. The follow-up exists to catch timing, not to wear people down. It references something new, not the same pitch repackaged.

The math shifted. Instead of 14 touches across 500 prospects, I send 3 touches to 150 prospects with much higher research per contact. Reply rates went up. Meetings went up. Spam complaints disappeared.

remixes.label: inbox-pollution-economics
remixes.hook: Your 14-step sequence isn't a strategy. It's a subsidy for bad targeting.
remixes.body:
Your 14-step sequence isn't a strategy. It's a subsidy for bad targeting.

Think about what a long sequence actually compensates for. If your ICP is tight and your messaging is relevant, you don't need 14 chances to get a reply. You need 2 or 3. The extra 11 emails exist because you're not confident email 1 will land. And the reason email 1 won't land is usually that the prospect shouldn't be in your list in the first place.

Long sequences mask targeting problems. They let you spray a loose list and hope that persistence covers for precision. It worked when inboxes were quieter. It doesn't work when your prospect gets 30 cold emails a day.

The economics are backwards too. Writing and sending 14 emails costs real money in tooling, deliverability risk, and domain reputation. Every irrelevant email you send makes the next one slightly less likely to land, across all your campaigns.

I flipped the ratio. Instead of spending 20% of effort on targeting and 80% on sequence writing, I spend 80% on targeting and 20% on a 3-email sequence. Better lists, better first emails, fewer touches, higher conversion.

The question isn't how many touches. It's whether touch 1 deserves a reply.

posts.title: The self-taught builder advantage
posts.hook: 18 months ago I was writing bash scripts and Googling "what is an API." Now I run my entire business on systems I built with coding agents.
posts.body:
18 months ago I was writing bash scripts and Googling "what is an API." Now I run my entire business on systems I built with coding agents.

Not because I became a 10x engineer. Because the bar for what you need to know dropped dramatically.

You don't need to understand memory management. You don't need to know how a compiler works. You need to understand data flow, system design at a high level, and how to describe what you want clearly enough that a coding agent can build it.

My background is plumbing. Ten years of it. The mental model transfers better than you'd think. Data flows through pipes. You need to know where the pressure is, where the joints leak, and how to route things efficiently.

The self-taught builders entering tech right now have an advantage the CS grads don't: they know what problems look like in the real world. They've done the manual version. They know which parts are painful because they've felt the pain.

That context is worth more than algorithmic knowledge when you're building business systems with AI.

The gap between "I have an idea" and "I have a working system" has never been smaller. The people who close that gap fastest aren't the ones with the best credentials. They're the ones with the clearest problem definition.

remixes.hook: The best builders I know right now aren't engineers. They're operators who learned to talk to coding agents.
remixes.body:
The best builders I know right now aren't engineers. They're operators who learned to talk to coding agents.

They can't write a binary search from scratch. They don't know what Big O notation means. But they understand their domain so deeply that when they describe what they need to a coding agent, the output is better than what a junior engineer would produce.

This is the part the "learn to code" crowd misses. The bottleneck was never syntax. It was knowing what to build and why. A former sales leader who spent 8 years watching CRM workflows break knows exactly what pipeline automation should look like. A former recruiter who processed 10,000 applications knows what a screening system needs to handle.

Domain expertise is the new technical advantage. The coding agent handles implementation. You handle the "what" and "why." And it turns out the "what" and "why" were always the hard part.

18 months ago I was Googling "what is an API." Now I run my entire business on custom-built systems. Not because I learned computer science. Because I learned how to decompose problems clearly enough that an AI could implement them.

The gap between "idea" and "working software" collapsed. The people who benefit most aren't career engineers. They're domain experts who finally have access to the tools.

remixes.label: learning-curve-collapse
remixes.hook: The traditional path from zero to building production software was 2 to 4 years. It took me 18 months. The next person will do it in 6.
remixes.body:
The traditional path from zero to building production software was 2 to 4 years. It took me 18 months. The next person will do it in 6.

The learning curve didn't flatten. It collapsed. And it collapsed unevenly in a way that favors a specific type of person.

You still need to understand how systems connect. Data flows in, gets transformed, goes somewhere. APIs talk to each other. Databases store state. If you can hold that mental model, you can build real things now.

What you don't need: 4 years of computer science fundamentals. You don't need to understand memory management, compiler design, or algorithm complexity. Those matter for infrastructure engineers. They don't matter for building business tools, automations, and workflows.

18 months ago I was writing bash scripts and Googling basic concepts. Now I have a monorepo with multiple production sites, automated pipelines, and a content OS that runs on systems I designed.

The key skill wasn't coding. It was learning to think in systems and communicate precisely with tools that can implement those systems. Clear problem decomposition. Good taste in architecture. Knowing what "done" looks like.

If you're a business operator, PM, or anyone who deeply understands a workflow, you're closer to building real software than you think.

posts.title: Stop applying, start building in public
posts.hook: Applying to 20 jobs a day is a volume play against a system that rewards specificity. The math doesn't work.
posts.body:
Applying to 20 jobs a day is a volume play against a system that rewards specificity. The math doesn't work.

I talk to people making career pivots into tech every week. The ones who land aren't the ones with the most applications out. They're the ones who built something specific and talked about it publicly.

A portfolio project that solves a real problem you actually had. A write-up about how you built it, what broke, what you learned. Three LinkedIn posts about the process.

That stack beats 200 applications because it does something a resume can't: it shows how you think.

Hiring managers scroll LinkedIn too. They see someone building in public, explaining their decisions, showing real work... that's a signal that cuts through the noise of 400 identical applications in their ATS.

The uncomfortable math: 20 applications/day x 30 days = 600 applications, maybe 10 responses, maybe 2 interviews. One build-in-public project with 5 posts about it = inbound from people who already know your work.

I got my first clients not from cold outreach but from people who watched me build my GTM stack in public. They saw the work. They didn't need to be convinced.

The job search version of this is the same. Build something. Talk about it. Let the work be the resume.

remixes.hook: Resumes tell me what you've done. A public build log tells me how you think.
remixes.body:
Resumes tell me what you've done. A public build log tells me how you think.

I've been on both sides of hiring conversations in tech. The candidates who stand out aren't the ones with the longest experience sections. They're the ones who can point to something they built and walk me through every decision they made.

Why did you choose this architecture? What broke? How did you fix it? What would you do differently? Those answers tell me more than 10 years of bullet points.

Building in public creates this artifact automatically. Every post about a technical decision, every thread about a bug you solved, every write-up about a project that failed. It's a living portfolio that demonstrates judgment, not just skills.

The people I see making successful career pivots right now are doing exactly this. They pick a specific problem. They build something real that addresses it. They document the process publicly. Not for clout. For proof.

A portfolio project that solves your own real problem beats 50 LeetCode completions. A write-up about how you debugged a production issue beats a certification. Hiring managers want evidence of thinking, and building in public is thinking out loud.

The job market rewards specificity. "Full-stack developer" is a commodity. "The person who built an open-source tool for managing restaurant inventory and wrote about every tradeoff" is memorable.

remixes.label: application-math-is-broken
remixes.hook: You applied to 200 jobs last month and got 3 responses. A friend shipped one project, posted about it twice, and got 5 inbound messages.
remixes.body:
You applied to 200 jobs last month and got 3 responses. A friend shipped one project, posted about it twice, and got 5 inbound messages.

The application game is a volume play against a system designed for specificity. ATS filters reward keyword matching, not capability. Recruiters spend 6 seconds per resume. You're competing with 400 other applicants for the same role.

Flip the model. Instead of optimizing your resume for every job description, build one thing that demonstrates exactly what you can do. Make it specific to a real problem. Talk about it publicly.

I see this pattern every week with career pivoters. The ones who land roles aren't spraying applications. They built a tool that automated something tedious in their previous job. They wrote a post about a technical challenge they solved. A hiring manager saw it and reached out.

This works because it inverts the power dynamic. Applications put you in a queue. Building in public puts you on a stage. The audience is smaller, but it's the right audience.

The uncomfortable part: it takes more effort per attempt. One thoughtful project with a write-up takes more time than 20 one-click applications. But the conversion rate is dramatically higher, and you build real skills in the process instead of just optimizing keywords.

Stop competing in the queue. Build your way out of it.
